results.name: fine_proximity_gradient
results.description: Among non-example targets within 10 of the nearest example, yes rate at distance 1-3 minus at distance 4-10; observed above null means human generalisation decays over short numerical distances more steeply than the model's interval hypotheses predict, below null means flatter.
results.code:
# name: fine_proximity_gradient
# description: Among non-example targets within 10 of the nearest example, yes rate at distance 1-3 minus at distance 4-10; observed above null means human generalisation decays over short numerical distances more steeply than the model's interval hypotheses predict, below null means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    a = r[nonmember & (nearest <= 3)]
    b = r[nonmember & (nearest >= 4) & (nearest <= 10)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: outlier_example_neighborhood
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly one example breaks the majority last digit, yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of that outlier example that do not end in the majority digit; observed above null means people treat the exceptional example as a genuine member and generalise around it (e.g. 27 -> 20s) more than the model, which discounts it as noise.
results.code:
# name: outlier_example_neighborhood
# description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly one example breaks the majority last digit, yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of that outlier example that do not end in the majority digit; observed above null means people treat the exceptional example as a genuine member and generalise around it (e.g. 27 -> 20s) more than the model, which discounts it as noise.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    ld = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 10), np.nan)
    cnt = np.zeros((len(t), 10))
    for d in range(10):
        cnt[:, d] = (ld == d).sum(axis=1)
    maj = cnt.argmax(axis=1)
    majc = cnt.max(axis=1)
    is_out = valid & (ld != maj[:, None])
    dout = np.where(is_out, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf).min(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (majc == n - 1) & nonmember & (dout <= 3) & (np.mod(t, 10) != maj)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: any_shared_digit_far
results.description: Among non-example targets more than 5 from the nearest example, yes rate for targets sharing any digit (either position) with at least one example minus targets sharing no digit with any example; observed above null means people use digit-level similarity to individual examples more than the model's whole-rule hypotheses predict.
results.code:
# name: any_shared_digit_far
# description: Among non-example targets more than 5 from the nearest example, yes rate for targets sharing any digit (either position) with at least one example minus targets sharing no digit with any example; observed above null means people use digit-level similarity to individual examples more than the model's whole-rule hypotheses predict.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    def digits(x):
        x = np.nan_to_num(x, nan=-1)
        o = np.where(x >= 0, np.mod(x, 10), -1)
        tdig = np.where(x >= 10, np.mod(np.floor(x / 10), 10), -2)
        h = np.where(x >= 100, 1, -3)
        return o, tdig, h
    eo, et, eh = digits(ex)
    to, tt, th = digits(t[:, None])
    share = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for a in (eo, et, eh):
        for b in (to, tt, th):
            share |= ((a == b) & (a >= 0) & valid).any(axis=1)
    m = nonmember & (nearest > 5)
    a_, b_ = r[m & share], r[m & ~share]
    if len(a_) == 0 or len(b_) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a_.mean() - b_.mean())

results.name: set_breadth_spread
results.description: Standard deviation across example sets (with >=20 responses) of each set's mean yes rate; observed above null means sets differ in how broadly people generalise more than the model predicts (some sets near-zero, others very broad), below null means less.

results.name: cell_unanimity
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells with >=2 responses in which all responses agree; observed above null means responses are more deterministic/extreme (closer to 0 or 1 per item) than the model's graded posterior predicts, below null means more disagreement.

results.name: majority_last_digit_far_target
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly n-1 examples share a last digit d (one exception), yes rate among non-example targets ending in d that are >4 from every example; observed above null means people extend a partly shared last digit to distant targets more than the fitted exception-tolerant model predicts, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: majority_last_digit_far_target
# description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly n-1 examples share a last digit d (one exception), yes rate among non-example targets ending in d that are >4 from every example; observed above null means people extend a partly shared last digit to distant targets more than the fitted exception-tolerant model predicts, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    ld = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 10), np.nan)
    tl = np.mod(t, 10)
    cnt = np.zeros((len(t), 10))
    for d in range(10):
        cnt[:, d] = (ld == d).sum(axis=1)
    maj = cnt.argmax(axis=1)
    majc = cnt.max(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (majc == n - 1) & (tl == maj) & nonmember & (nearest > 4)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: unrelated_target_floor
results.description: Yes rate among targets more than 10 from every example, sharing no last digit with any example, and not divisible by the examples' gcd when that gcd is >=2 (or any target when gcd is 1); observed above null means a larger lapse/noise floor of yes to unrelated numbers than the model predicts, below null means a smaller one.
results.code:
# name: unrelated_target_floor
# description: Yes rate among targets more than 10 from every example, sharing no last digit with any example, and not divisible by the examples' gcd when that gcd is >=2 (or any target when gcd is 1); observed above null means a larger lapse/noise floor of yes to unrelated numbers than the model predicts, below null means a smaller one.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    nearest = dist.min(axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    ei = np.where(valid, ex, 0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(ei, axis=1)
    ti = t.astype(np.int64)
    div = (g >= 2) & (np.mod(ti, np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0)
    same_ld = (valid & (np.mod(np.nan_to_num(ex), 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    m = nonmember & (nearest > 10) & ~same_ld & ~div
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: single_example_far_yes_rate
results.description: For sets with exactly one example, yes rate among targets more than 10 from the example; observed above null means people generalise from a single example to distant numbers more broadly than the model predicts, below null means more narrowly.
